title: The Yoginī's Embrace
summary: The poet asks a yoginī to press the tiaḍḍā and embrace him, and to rub lotus and vajra together in the evening; without her he cannot live a moment, and kissing her mouth he drinks lotus nectar. Flowing through the maṇikula she comes to Oḍḍiyāna; key and lock go into the mother-in-law's house, the braid of moon and sun is split at its sides, and Guṇḍarīpāda, a hero in kundura, raises his flag among men and women. Munidatta reads the yoginī as Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtī, the tiaḍḍā as the three channels and the lotus nectar as ultimate bodhicitta, and takes the song as moving from union through the purification of body, speech and mind to the siddha's display of his powers (cp.04.m2–cp.04.m6).

flags.note: The heading line itself reads only rāga aru. I added the poet's name from the attribution guṇḍarīpādānāṃ, 'of Guṇḍarīpāda', which the manuscript writes before the first line (the edition's emendation takes it out of 1a), and from the Tibetan heading, which ends guN+Di ri'i zhabs kyi'o, 'of Guṇḍaripāda'. Drop it if headings should render only the heading line.

lines.gloss: tiaḍḍā (sense uncertain) · having pressed · O yoginī · give · embrace

flags.note: tiaḍḍā is unexplained. Its first element is probably ti-, 'three'. Munidatta quotes it as tiyaṛa and takes it as the three channels (cp.04.m2); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ka mgo, literally perhaps 'top of a pillar', whose sense here is unclear. Kept in source form, as the glossary directs.

cāpī is an absolutive, 'having pressed'. I take its subject to be the yoginī, who is also the subject of the imperative de, 'give'. The Tibetan agrees in reading two commands (ka mgo non la ... byin, 'press the ka mgo and give'). Munidatta's cāpayitvā (cp.04.m2) does not say who presses. 'me' is supplied: the Bengali has no pronoun after de.
The Tibetan line, /ka mgo non la yan lag 'khyud la byin/, has no word for joini, 'yoginī'. It renders aṅkabālī as yan lag 'khyud, 'embrace of the limbs', which supports 'embrace'.

ghāṇṭa: taken as 'rubbing, churning' (compare Sanskrit ghaṭṭana, 'rubbing', and Bengali ghā̃ṭā, 'to stir'), in line with Munidatta's ghṛṣṭi, 'rubbing' (cp.04.m2). A reading ghaṇṭā, 'bell', the ritual partner of the vajra, is conceivable but fits karahũ, 'do', poorly. The Tibetan has sbyor, 'joining': /chu skyes rdo rje sbyor tshod .../.

karahũ: taken as an imperative, as Munidatta (kuru) and the Tibetan (gyis) take it. It could also be a first person plural, 'let us make the rubbing'. The song does not name the addressee. Munidatta addresses this line to 'best of yogis' (bho yogivara; Tibetan kye'i mchog gi rnal 'byor pa), a man, although 1a speaks to the yoginī. I have not harmonized the two.

biālī: 'evening' (Sanskrit vikāla), as the glossary has it. Munidatta takes it as vi-kāla, 'free of time' (cp.04.m2). The Tibetan line gives both senses side by side: dus min, 'not the time', and dgongs mo, 'evening'.

Shastri prints ধ্রু after this line as well as after 2b, 3b and 4b. If ধ্রু follows the refrain and every later couplet, the pattern makes couplet 1, not couplet 2, the refrain. Munidatta calls neither couplet the refrain, and his count (couplet 4 is his 'third pada', cp.04.m5) fits either. I have followed the input, which marks couplet 2 as the refrain.

lines.translit: joini tam̐i binu khanahim̐ na jībami
lines.gloss: O yoginī · you · without · even for a moment · not · I live
lines.en: [Yoginī]{yogini}, without you I cannot live a moment;

flags.note: na jībami is literally 'I do not live'; 'cannot live' is the English idiom. Munidatta's paraphrase also speaks of inability: 'I am not able to hold the breath of life' (cp.04.m3). The Tibetan has mi 'tsho, 'do not live'.

lines.translit: to muha cumbī kamalarasa pībami || dhru ||
lines.gloss: your · mouth · having kissed · lotus-juice · I drink
lines.en: kissing your mouth, I drink [lotus nectar]{kamala-rasa}.

flags.note: muha can be 'mouth' or 'face'; 'mouth' suits the kiss. Munidatta's vaktra (cp.04.m3) and the Tibetan zhal carry the same double sense.

lines.gloss: throw (imperative?) · O yoginī · smearing · not · goes (= cannot happen)

flags.note: The line is obscure. khem̐pahu is from kṣip-, 'throw, cast'. I read it as an imperative addressed to the yoginī, with no object stated. It could also be a present, 'you throw', or carry the Bengali sense 'pass (time)'. lepa na jāya, with the passive idiom 'X does not go', means 'smearing does not happen', 'nothing sticks'. Munidatta reads kṣepa, 'casting', as union in her own place, and speaks of the yoginī and the stain of delusion (cp.04.m4). Alternatives: 'You throw, yoginī, and no stain clings'; 'Cast it, yoginī: it cannot be smeared'.

The Tibetan (Toh 2293) reads /'phangs nas len mi shes pa rnal 'byor ma/, 'the yoginī who, having thrown, does not know how to take (back)', as though its text had a form of le-, 'take', where Shastri prints lepa, 'smearing'. I follow the Bengali, which Munidatta's gloss on staining supports.

lines.gloss: in the maṇikula · having flowed · in Oḍḍiyāna · joined (?)

flags.note: maṇikula is uncertain: maṇi, 'jewel', with kula, 'family, clan', or kūla, 'bank' ('on the jewel bank'). Munidatta's paraphrase has maṇimūla, 'the root of the jewel', in its place (cp.04.m4). The Tibetan transcribes ma Ni kuN+Da li, perhaps from a reading maṇikuṇḍali.

bahiā is taken as the absolutive of bah-, 'flow, be carried'. The Tibetan has phyir, 'outside', as though reading bāhira ('outside the maṇikula'). sagāa is taken as from saṃgata, 'come together, joined'. Munidatta has antarbhavati, 'is absorbed within', and the Tibetan has mnyam, 'equal, together'. The song does not state the subject; Munidatta makes it the yoginī. I have not supplied a pronoun.

lines.gloss: mother-in-law · in the house · having put · key · lock

flags.note: ghāli is an absolutive, 'having put'. I render it as a participle leading into the imperative of 4b. Neither line names who acts.

The Tibetan reads /sgyug mo'i khyim phyin lde kyog lde mig go/, 'gone to the mother-in-law's house: hooked key, key'. It has phyin, 'having gone', where the Bengali has ghāli, 'having put', and it renders tāla, 'lock', with lde mig, which usually means 'key'. I follow the Bengali; Munidatta's gloss on sealing the lock (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa, cp.04.m5) supports 'lock'.

lines.en: split the [sides]{paksa} of the [braid]{veni} of [moon]{moon} and [sun]{surya}.

flags.note: Each word is uncertain. beṇi is taken as 'braid' (Sanskrit veṇī), a word that also means a meeting of rivers; pakhā as 'wings, sides' (Sanskrit pakṣa); phāla as the imperative 'split, tear'. Munidatta supports the last two: 'having broken (khaṇḍayitvā) the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) of moon and sun' (cp.04.m5). He does not gloss beṇi.

The Tibetan reads /zla ba nyi ma gnyis kyi sgo glegs can/, '(the house) with the door-panels of the two, moon and sun'. It takes beṇi as 'the two' and pakhā as the leaves of a door, and has no verb for phāla. That reading suits the key and lock of 4a and would give a quite different line ('whose door-leaves are moon and sun'). I follow the Bengali and Munidatta.

lines.gloss: says · Guḍarī · I · in kundura · hero

flags.note: The poet names himself Guḍarī, without the honorific -pāda that the glossary form Guṇḍarīpāda carries. I have used the approved form as instructed. 'Guḍarī says' would keep the self-naming as the song has it (see questions).
The Tibetan has /guN+Da rI bdag kun+Da re pa smras/, 'Guṇḍarī says: I am one of kundare', with no word for 'hero' (bīrā). Munidatta's gloss has vīro'ham, 'I am a hero' (cp.04.m6).
kundure is locative, 'in kundura'; Munidatta's kundureṇa is instrumental, 'by kundura' (cp.04.m6).

lines.en: among men and women I have raised the [flag]{cira}.

flags.note: ubhila, 'raised, set upright', does not mark person. 'I' is carried over from ahme in 5a and agrees with Munidatta's mayoddhṛtam, 'raised by me' (cp.04.m6).
cīrā is a strip of cloth or rag, raised here like a flag, as the glossary has it. The Tibetan renders it rtags mtshan, 'sign, emblem', with the verb btsugs, 'planted'.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song names the rāga it is sung to. The melody Aru is not otherwise known. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls it skya rengs, 'dawn', as if the name were Sanskrit aruṇa, 'dawn-red'.

Munidatta introduces the song as continuing the point of song 3: Guṇḍarīpāda, through understanding the conduct of Śrī Heruka, teaches others that things are without intrinsic nature. The Tibetan has 'the realization of Śrī Heruka' (dpal he ru ka'i rtogs pa), with no word for 'conduct'.
tiaḍḍā: a word of uncertain sense, kept in source form. Its first element is probably ti-, 'three'. Munidatta quotes it as tiyaṛa; the Tibetan translation has ka mgo.

Munidatta reads the tiaḍḍā as the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā. Once they have been pressed and made free of appearance, he says, she herself is the purified avadhūtikā, the selfless yoginī (nirātmayoginī). He explains the embrace (aṅkavālī) as aṅka, 'mark', and pāl-, 'protect': she gives her own mark to the practitioner and protects it. As an alternative, he says that through union marked by the moments beginning with vicitra she gives the sequence of joys. He addresses the rubbing of lotus and vajra to 'best of yogis' and takes biālī as vi-kāla: realize directly the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is free of time.

The Tibetan translation of this comment (Toh 2293) differs from the Sanskrit in three places. The three channels are made shin du gsal snang, 'very clearly appearing', where the Sanskrit has nirābhāsīkṛtya, 'made free of appearance'. The yoginī 'moves' the mark (skyod par byed) where the Sanskrit has pālayati, 'protects'; skyod may be a slip for skyong, 'protect'. And sgom pa po, 'meditator', stands where the Sanskrit has tāvaka, 'your devotee'. That suggests a reading bhāvaka, the word the Sanskrit comment ends with.

vajra: the thunderbolt-diamond of Indian myth and the ritual sceptre modelled on it, the emblem of the indestructible in tantric Buddhism; the song's word is kuliśa. The yoginī tantras pair lotus and vajra as female and male in union. Munidatta speaks here of 'the rubbing of the union of vajra and lotus'.

Munidatta has the poet address the yoginī as Nairātmā ('O selfless yoginī') and paraphrases the refrain: without you, not even for a moment can I hold the breath of life (prāṇavāta), so irresistibly swift and restless is it. He backs this with a scriptural verse: in arising, abiding and ceasing, and in intermediate existence, all conceptual thought in the world is the play of wind and mind. He calls her mouth innate joy. The lotus nectar he calls the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus, ultimate bodhicitta, which he says he makes, through the guru's lineage, at the time of kāliñjara, the joy of cessation. He quotes the Hevajra: 'The unfit is called ḍiṇḍima, the fit, great kāliñjara.'

The Tibetan quotation of 2a has rnal 'byor without the feminine ma, probably for metre; its comment has the feminine (bdag med rnal 'byor ma). In the comment the Tibetan renders viramānanda, 'joy of cessation', as sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, 'joy of variety', and translates kāliñjara by its sense, skal ba dang ldan pa, 'fortunate'.

Munidatta calls this couplet the praise of the yoginī. He glosses khepa as kṣepa, 'casting', which he explains as union in her own place. The selfless yoginī in the form of bodhicitta, through the joy purified by vilakṣaṇa, at the root of the jewel, becomes [un]stained by the stain of delusion (see the witness note). Then, having enjoyed the taste of play there, she goes up and up from the root of the jewel and is absorbed into the wheel of great bliss. He quotes a verse of Kṛṣṇācārya that calls this 'the best of mountains' and 'the place of great bliss'. His paraphrase has the root of the jewel where the song has maṇikula, and the wheel of great bliss where it has Oḍḍiyāna, but he glosses neither word explicitly.

Munidatta's Sanskrit as printed, mohamalāvaliptā, most naturally divides as mohamala-avaliptā, 'smeared with the stain of delusion', which runs against the song's 'no stain clings'. The Tibetan has rmongs pa'i dri mas ma gos par 'gyur ro, 'becomes unstained by the stain of delusion', with a negative, so its Sanskrit may have read -āliptā or -anavaliptā. Either way, the translation of 3a follows the song.

maṇikula: a word of uncertain sense, kept in source form. Maṇi is 'jewel'; kula is 'family, clan' or, as elsewhere in the songs, kūla, 'bank'. Oḍḍiyāna, where the line ends, is a land famed in tantric Buddhism as a seat of yoginīs, usually placed in the Swat valley.

The couplet sets a domestic scene: key and lock are put away in the house of the mother-in-law, the figure of authority over a young wife in a joint household. The song does not say who puts them there. The braid made of moon and sun is the song's own image, and the translation keeps it as a braid.

Munidatta says this 'third verse' teaches purification. First the lord of yogis makes the vajra of body firm, beginning with deity yoga. By the instruction in vajra recitation he breaks the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) of moon and sun and steadies the vajra of speech. Then, to make the vajra of mind firm, he leads the avadhūtikā of the joy of cessation, one in taste with innate joy, to the house of breath (śvāsam āgāraṃ), the summit of Sumeru. On the key: in sealing the lock, the door of the root of the jewel is to be blocked. He supports this with a verse of Kṛṣṇācārya in which a firm lock is set at the door of the sky, where mind and wind are.

The printed Sanskrit of this comment reads sahajānandaikalolībhāvaṃ na śvāsam āgāraṃ, with a negative that makes no sense. The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba dang ro gcig pa'i ngo bos dbugs kyi khyim du, 'by its nature of one taste with innate joy, to the house of breath', which suggests -bhāvena and no negative. Munidatta's śvāsam āgāraṃ, 'breath' and 'house', seems to echo the song's sāsu gharẽ, 'the mother-in-law's house'.

beṇi, 'braid' (Sanskrit veṇī), is also the word for a meeting of rivers, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga. pakhā, Sanskrit pakṣa, is 'wing, side, flank', and also 'half', as of a lunar month. phāla is taken as the imperative of phāl-, 'split, tear'. The Tibetan construes the line quite differently (see the flags on 4b).

kundura: a word the tantras use for the sexual union of yogic practice, usually spelled kunduru; in ordinary Sanskrit kunduru is olibanum, a fragrant resin. The Tibetan translation keeps the word (kun+Da re). The poet's name has several spellings: the song has Guḍarī; Munidatta has Guḍḍarī and Guṇḍarīpāda, as does the attribution before the song; the Tibetan has guN+Di ri and guN+Da rI.

Munidatta says Guḍḍarī praises himself because he has directly realized the vajra-like samādhi. He takes the 'men and women' as the other yogins and yoginīs, those turned away from the guru's lineage. Among them the poet is a hero because, by kundura, the imperishable bliss of the yoga of union of the two organs, he crushes the enemy, the afflictions. Among them too he has raised the cloth (cīra), the mark of the lord of yogis, the eightfold mastery and the rest, to display the higher knowledges.

termsOmitted.reason: Detected only in the Tibetan, whose khyim renders the Bengali ghara. The translation follows the Bengali word, which is rendered with the house entry.

Detected only in the Tibetan quotation, which has rnal 'byor without the feminine ma, probably for metre. The Bengali has the feminine vocative joini, rendered with the yoginī entry, and Munidatta's gloss is feminine in both languages (cp.04.m3).

proposals.definition: A braid or plait of hair (Sanskrit veṇī); the same word names the meeting of rivers, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga. In song 4 the moon and the sun form a braid whose sides are to be split. The Tibetan translation has gnyis, 'the two', where the Bengali has beṇi.
proposals.symbolicImage: a braid made of the moon and the sun
proposals.rationale: A concrete image in song 4 that the glossary lacks; an entry keeps its rendering fixed if it recurs. Munidatta does not gloss beṇi itself, so no reading is recorded.

proposals.definition: Wing, side or flank (Sanskrit pakṣa, Old Bengali pakhā); also half of a lunar month, and a party in a dispute. In song 4 the sides of the braid of moon and sun are to be split; the Tibetan translation renders the word there as sgo glegs, 'door-panel'. Munidatta speaks of the 'taking of sides' (pakṣagraha).
proposals.symbolicImage: the sides of the braid of moon and sun, which are to be split

symbolicReadings.referent: the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) by the moon and the sun, which the lord of yogis breaks through the instruction in vajra recitation, so steadying the vajra of speech

proposals.rationale: The word recurs: according to the emptiness entry, Munidatta renders song 1's sunupākha as śūnyatāpakṣa, 'the side of emptiness', and here pakhā carries a reading of its own. One entry keeps 'side' consistent.

proposals.definition: Delusion or bewilderment (moha): with desire and hatred, one of the three root afflictions of Buddhist teaching, the confusion that hides how things are. Munidatta speaks of the stain of delusion (mohamala) in describing the yoginī (cp.04.m4); the Tibetan has rmongs pa.
proposals.rationale: A recurring doctrinal term of the commentary that the glossary lacks; distinct from ignorance (avidyā).

proposals.definition: The vajra of body, of speech and of mind: a buddha's body, speech and mind, which tantric practice aims to make the practitioner's own. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes the vajra of body firm through deity yoga, steadies the vajra of speech by vajra recitation, then works to make the vajra of mind firm (cp.04.m5).
proposals.rationale: A recurring triad of tantric commentary, named member by member in cp.04.m5; one entry keeps the three renderings parallel.

questions: Bhaṇitā name (5a): the glossary's Guṇḍarīpāda carries the honorific -pāda, which a poet would hardly use of himself, and the song has Guḍarī. May the entry take 'Guḍarī' (or 'Guṇḍarī') as a variant for the self-naming line, so that 5a reads 'Guḍarī says…'?

Refrain: Shastri prints ধ্রু after 1b as well as after 2b, 3b and 4b, which would make couplet 1 the refrain rather than couplet 2. Munidatta's count fits either. Should the refrain marking be checked against the manuscript?

3a is the line I am least sure of. Is 'Throw, yoginī: no stain clings' acceptable? The alternatives are a present ('You throw, yoginī, and no stain clings') or the Tibetan's sense ('having thrown, she does not know how to take it back').

4b: I follow Munidatta ('split the sides of the braid of moon and sun'). The Tibetan's 'with the door-panels of the two, moon and sun' fits the key and lock of 4a well. Should that reading stay in the notes, or be considered for the line itself?
Heading: I added Guṇḍarīpāda from the attribution before the song and from the Tibetan heading. Keep it, or render only 'Rāga Aru'?

1b: Munidatta addresses the line to a man ('best of yogis'), while the song speaks to the yoginī in 1a. I have left the line's addressee unnamed and flagged the divergence. Is that the handling you want?

1b: the glossary renders vikala as 'evening'. Given Munidatta's 'free of time' and the Tibetan's double rendering (dus min and dgongs mo), is 'evening' still right in the line, with the other senses in the notes?
1a: 'give me an embrace' supplies 'me', which the Bengali leaves implicit. Acceptable, or would you prefer 'give an embrace'?

Proposals: I have proposed 'braid' (veni) and 'side' (paksa) for 4b, 'delusion' (moha) and 'three vajras' (trivajra) from the commentary. Is 'side' the right headword for pakṣa across the songs, given song 1's sunupākha?
